chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Zurarah and Muhammad ibn Muslim and Abu Basir and Burayd and al-Fudayl, from Abu Ja'far and Abu Abdillah (peace be upon them both), who said:

Regarding cattle: in every thirty cows, one young cow that has completed its first year (tabi' hasan) is due; and there is nothing less than that. In forty cows, one mature cow (musinnah) is due; and there is nothing between thirty and forty until it reaches forty. When it reaches forty, one mature cow is due. There is nothing between forty and sixty. When it reaches sixty, two young cows are due until seventy. When it reaches seventy, one young cow and one mature cow are due until eighty. When it reaches eighty, in every forty, one mature cow is due. When it reaches ninety, three young cows are due. When it reaches one hundred and twenty, in every forty, one mature cow is due. Then the cattle return to their age classifications. There is nothing due on the 'nayyif' (extra beyond the round number), nor on the fractions, nor on the workers. The charity (khums/zakat) is only on the grazing cattle. And whatever has not completed the year with its owner, there is nothing due upon it until the year completes. When the year completes, it becomes obligatory upon it.

key_terms.السَّائِمَةُ الرَّاعِيَةُ: Grazing cattle that feed on natural pasture
key_terms.النَّيِّفُ: The extra number beyond a round ten (e.g., 31-39)
key_terms.بَقَرَةٌ مُسِنَّةٌ: A mature cow, typically in its fourth year
key_terms.تَبِيعٌ حَوْلِيٌّ: A young cow that has completed its first year

ai.seo_question: What is the exact calculation for zakat on cattle according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elaborates on the *khums*-like structure of cattle zakat, detailing the precise thresholds for *tabi'* (one-year-old) and *musinnah* (four-year-old) animals, a system often compared to the zakat of camels and sheep in Shia jurisprudence. It emphasizes that the obligation is strictly tied to the *saimah* (grazing cattle) and requires the full lunar year (*hawl*) to have passed, excluding partial counts or fractional years from liability. This textual precision underscores the Shia scholarly focus on exact numerical criteria in ritual finance, distinguishing it from broader generalizations found in other schools.
